claims.text: The starting material is bulk CoCrFeNi with a homogeneous microstructure.
Laser surface alloying with a minor Ti or Nb addition is the proposed intervention.
A laser power of 200–300 W can treat the top 10–20 μm of the alloy appropriately.
Laser surface alloying of CoCrFeNi with Ti or Nb will produce a graded, nanohierarchical, compositionally undulated surface layer.
The modified surface will contain nanoscale Ti- or Nb-rich secondary-phase precipitates in a re-solidified CoCrFeNi matrix.
Rapid solidification during laser surface alloying creates the tailored near-surface structure.
Nanoprecipitates reinforce and harden the worn surface at lower temperatures.
At higher sliding temperatures, tribochemical reactions become an adaptive component of interface protection.
High-temperature sliding will generate a dense, continuous, nanocrystalline oxide glaze on the modified CoCrFeNi surface.
The oxide glaze will act as a self-lubricating barrier that minimizes adhesive and oxidative wear.
The combined nanohierarchical architecture and adaptive tribo-reaction will maintain reduced wear from room temperature to 800 °C.
The modified alloy will maintain a coefficient of friction below approximately 0.25 across the full temperature range.
The modified alloy will have lower friction and wear than untreated CoCrFeNi throughout the full temperature range.
Untreated CoCrFeNi exhibits higher friction and accelerated wear, especially at temperature extremes.
The proposed operating boundary is ambient-air sliding from room temperature to 800 °C under approximately 5–10 N.
The stability of the laser-induced nanostructure and oxide glaze may depend on sliding duration and process variations.
A controlled comparison of laser-alloyed and untreated CoCrFeNi samples can test the hypothesis using friction, wear, and post-test microscopy measurements.
Failure to achieve at least a 20% reduction in average friction coefficient and a statistically significant wear reduction across the full range is designated as a falsifying result.
Absence of nanoprecipitates or a continuous glaze layer after testing is designated as a falsifying result.
